title: A hundred times a day
hook: balihaaree gur aapne: I'm a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of men (Asa di Var, ang 462)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhunee, and your line: old tunes, new words. Did an old habit get a new purpose? Today Asa di Var opens its mouth, and its very first words are thanks. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Ask people about a teacher who changed their life and watch their faces. A high school English teacher who said, you can write. A coach who saw something before anyone else did. A grandmother who taught them to pray, or to cook, or to forgive. Plenty of those teachers never heard a real thank-you, or heard it once, years too late. Guru Nanak opens his great ballad not with God's power, not with a warning, but with a thank-you to the Guru, said a hundred times a day.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CHANGED A LIFE.` → `WE RARELY SAY THANK YOU.` → `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The first salok of Asa di Var, in paraphrase: I am a sacrifice to my Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels out of human beings, and took no time to do it. Balihaaree is the first word. It means I am a sacrifice to you, I'd give myself for you. It's the language of overflowing love and gratitude, the kind a mother might whisper over a child. Diuhaarree sad vaar: in a day, a hundred times. Not once, at a graduation. Over and over, every day. Then the reason. Maanas te devte: from humans, devtas, angels or godlike beings. The Guru's teaching takes ordinary, struggling people and makes them shine. And karat na laagee vaar: in the doing of it, there was no delay. Listen to that last word, vaar. Here it means delay. Just before, sad vaar meant a hundred times. And the whole bani is a var, a ballad. Some listeners hear a play on that sound in the very first salok. Who is the Guru here? For Guru Nanak, the true Guru is ultimately God, the Word that teaches from within; Sikhs also honor the human Gurus who carried that Word, and today the Guru Granth Sahib itself. The salok doesn't separate them. It just overflows with thanks. And there's an idea folded in. The salok doesn't picture people climbing to the angels by sheer effort. It pictures a teacher who lifts. The first emotion of Asa di Var, before any argument, is gratitude for being lifted.
screen: `BALIHAAREE: I'D GIVE MYSELF FOR YOU.` · `A HUNDRED TIMES, EVERY DAY.` · `FROM HUMANS, ANGELS, WITHOUT DELAY.` · `GRATITUDE BEFORE ANY ARGUMENT.` · then, large: `MADE ANGELS OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your teacher. Sit and let one teacher come to mind: a schoolteacher, a parent, a mentor, an author, someone who lifted you. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they gave you. Then, silently, thank them, as fully as you can. If it rises, thank them again, and again. If you pray, you can also thank the Guru, or God, as the teacher behind all teachers, and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Balihaaree, I am a sacrifice to you: Asa di Var's first salok says balihaaree to the Guru a hundred times a day, who made angels of humans without delay.
Your line: made angels of men. Today, send one real thank-you message to a teacher who lifted you, even if it's years late. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Asa di Var opens with Guru Nanak's salok of gratitude to the Guru, balihaaree, a hundred times a day, sung in gurdwaras each morning.

options: gratitude to the Guru, a hundred times a day.

original.note: Gurmukhi: balihaaree, I am a sacrifice to you; a word of overflowing love and thanks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hundred times a day means saying thanks a lot.
what it means: overflowing gratitude to the Guru who lifts ordinary people into the light, without delay.
what a scholar hears: the salok rhymes sad vaar, a hundred times, with na laagee vaar, no delay, in a bani that is itself a var.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok 1 before pauri 1, Guru Nanak (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 462)

notes: Paraphrase of the opening salok (balihaaree gur aapne diuhaarree sad vaar; jin maanas te devte kee-e karat na laagee vaar): confirm.
The vaar wordplay is offered as something many listeners hear, not as a claim about the Guru's intent; check.
The note on who the Guru is (God as the true Guru, the human Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib) is brief; a Keeper may refine.

Fresh review: hook no longer tells the listener they never thanked anyone; 'many listeners' softened to 'some'; the claim about Sikh teaching as a whole narrowed to what the salok pictures (spoken text and myth).
